extraction_notes.note: Properties 1 and 2 (\newtheorem{prop}{Property}) are typed assumption, not claim: Theorem 3 takes them as hypotheses on the gene-tree law. Remark 2, which asserts they hold under the MSC and argues it, is retyped claim with its argument as a nested proof (PP6).

Lemma 8 has no proof environment; its justification (adapting Lemma 5.1 of Aizenbud et al. once T_E is ultrametric) is split between the text after the lemma (H.2) and Section H.3, emitted as two proof parts; Lemma 8 is marked semi_formal.

The multiplicativity claim's hypothesis sentence ('let v_1,v_2,v_3 ...') precedes the definition of the node similarity, so the claim starts at 'Then, ...' and the hypothesis is carried verbatim in assumptions.

The MSC coalescence conditions are one enumerate that introduces Delta^g_ij (and local path edges e_1..e_l); kept as one definition rather than split mid-list, against the one-symbol-per-sentence warning.
The prose proof of auxiliary Lemma 5 sits inside the proof of Lemma 1; the outer proof gets no setup step for it, since that step would duplicate PP10's span exactly.
pseudocode_steps returned an empty span for the \Return line; its statement is set to the verbatim printed text. \EndIf/\EndFor lines dropped.

Dataset descriptions, figure-only experiments (Appendices D, F, G) and the discussion's future work are not extracted; only headline numerical findings are claims. The introduction's contribution list is folded into also_stated_at of Theorem 3, Proposition 1 and the speedup claim.

The identity argmin |d_j - D(C_1,C_2)| = argmin |v_j - vbar^(2)| ('by simple linear algebra') is kept inside the outgroup-selection algorithm step, not as a separate claim; it needs the two k-means clusters to be separated on the Fiedler line.

Notation is inconsistent: alphabet size l (Sec. 2) vs d (Sec. 5.1); an unrooted species tree (Sec. 2) vs a rooted timed one (Def. 1); Appendix C writes S^g = S exp(-2 Delta) with distances D, while Sec. 5.1 gives S^g = exp(4 tr(Q) tau^g).

nodes.name: Concatenation Analysis using Maximum Likelihood (CA-ML)
nodes.statement: Perhaps one of the simplest ones is Concatenation Analysis using Maximum Likelihood (\texttt{CA-ML}). In this approach, the gene sequences of each species are concatenated, and the species tree is recovered by maximum likelihood.
nodes.statement_short: Concatenate all gene alignments and fit a single maximum-likelihood tree.
input: the gene sequences of each species

nodes.name: Concatenate genes
nodes.statement: the gene sequences of each species are concatenated
nodes.statement_short: Concatenate the gene alignments per species.

nodes.name: Maximum-likelihood tree
nodes.statement: the species tree is recovered by maximum likelihood
nodes.statement_short: Fit one ML tree to the concatenated alignment.

nodes.name: Statistical inconsistency of CA-ML under the MSC
nodes.statement: Indeed, \texttt{CA-ML} has been shown to be statistically inconsistent under the multispecies coalescent (MSC) model \cite{kubatko2007inconsistency,roch2015likelihood}.
conclusions: \texttt{CA-ML} has been shown to be statistically inconsistent under the multispecies coalescent (MSC) model

nodes.name: Summary methods
nodes.statement: A different approach to species tree reconstruction is to first estimate all the individual gene trees by some tree reconstruction method. Then, the species tree is inferred by summarizing information from all gene trees. Methods applying this approach are known as {\em summary methods}.
nodes.statement_short: Methods that first estimate each gene tree and then summarize them into a species tree.

nodes.name: Consistency of summary methods under the MSC
nodes.statement: These summary methods were proven to be consistent under the MSC model, assuming the input gene trees are estimated correctly \cite{allman2016species, liu2009estimating, vachaspati2015astrid, mirarab2014astral}.
nodes.origin_citation: Allman et al. 2016; Liu et al. 2009; Vachaspati & Warnow 2015; Mirarab et al. 2014
assumptions: assuming the input gene trees are estimated correctly
conclusions: These summary methods were proven to be consistent under the MSC model

nodes.name: uDance
nodes.statement: \texttt{uDance} \cite{balaban2024generation} offers an alternative divide-and-conquer strategy. It recovers a backbone tree from a subset of species and assigns each of the remaining species to an edge in the backbone tree. Then, the algorithm reconstructs a subtree for every group of species assigned to the same edge.
nodes.statement_short: Divide-and-conquer: backbone tree, place remaining species on its edges, rebuild a subtree per edge group.

nodes.name: Backbone tree
nodes.statement: It recovers a backbone tree from a subset of species
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct a backbone tree on a species subset.

nodes.name: Assign species to edges
nodes.statement: assigns each of the remaining species to an edge in the backbone tree
nodes.statement_short: Place each remaining species on a backbone edge.

nodes.name: Per-edge subtrees
nodes.statement: Then, the algorithm reconstructs a subtree for every group of species assigned to the same edge.
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct one subtree per edge group.

nodes.name: Unrooted binary species tree
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal T = (V, E)$ denote an unrooted binary species tree with $m$ terminal and $m-2$ non-terminal nodes. Terminal nodes correspond to present-day species, whereas non-terminal nodes to ancestor species.

nodes.name: Index sets of terminal and non-terminal nodes
nodes.statement: We denote the indices of the terminal nodes by $[m] \equiv \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and the non-terminal nodes by $\{m+1,\ldots,2m-2\}$.

nodes.name: Alphabet of sequence symbols
nodes.statement: The observed data for each current species at a specific gene is a sequence of symbols from a set $\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_\ell\}$. In the common DNA setting, $\ell = 4$ and the set is $\{A,C,G,T\}$ which are the four nucleotide bases.

nodes.name: Gene alignments $\{X^g\}_{g=1}^K$
nodes.statement: In the problem at hand, we are given a set of $K$ gene alignments, denoted $\{X^g\}_{g=1}^K$.

nodes.name: Gene alignment matrix
nodes.statement: A single gene alignment $X^g \in \{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_\ell\}^{m \times {n_g}}$ contains $m$ sequences of length $n_g$, where each sequence corresponds to a single species.

nodes.name: Species sequence $X_i^g$
nodes.statement: We denote by $X_i^g = (X_{i1}^g,\ldots,X_{in_g}^g)$ the sequence that corresponds to species $i$ in the $g$-th gene.

nodes.name: Species tree reconstruction from multiple gene alignments
nodes.statement: The goal is to reconstruct the species tree from these $K$ gene alignments.

nodes.name: Estimated evolutionary distance $\hat D^g$
nodes.statement: For each gene $g$ with gene alignment matrix $X^g$, we compute a measure of evolutionary distance $\hat D^g(i,j)$ between all pairs of observed species $(i,j)$.

nodes.name: Gene similarity matrix estimate $\hat S^g$
nodes.statement: Next, we compute the gene $m\times m$ similarity matrix between all $m$ species, via \begin{equation} \hat S^g(i,j) = \exp\big(-\hat D^g(i,j)\big), \qquad \forall i,j \in [m]. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Similarity from distance
nodes.statement: \hat S^g(i,j) = \exp\big(-\hat D^g(i,j)\big), \qquad \forall i,j \in [m].
nodes.label: eq:similarity

nodes.name: Degree matrix $A^g$
nodes.statement: Let $A^{g}$ denote the diagonal matrix with entries $A^{g}(i,i) = \sum_{j=1}^m \hat S^g(i,j)$.

nodes.name: Normalized graph Laplacian $L^g$
nodes.statement: The normalized Laplacian $L^{g}$ of the similarity graph is defined by, \begin{equation} L^{g} = I - (A^{g})^{-0.5} \hat S^g (A^{g})^{-0.5}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Laplacian of a connected graph is PSD with simple zero eigenvalue
nodes.statement: For any connected graph, the Laplacian matrix is positive semi-definite with a zero eigenvalue with multiplicity one.
assumptions: For any connected graph
conclusions: the Laplacian matrix is positive semi-definite with a zero eigenvalue with multiplicity one

nodes.name: Fiedler vector
nodes.statement: The Fiedler vector is the eigenvector of $L$ that corresponds to its smallest non-zero eigenvalue.
differentia: corresponds to its smallest non-zero eigenvalue

nodes.name: Clan
nodes.statement: A subset of nodes $C$ in a tree $\mathcal T$ is a {\em clan} if it can be separated from the rest of the tree by removing a single edge $e$.
nodes.genus: subset of nodes $C$ in a tree $\mathcal T$
differentia: it can be separated from the rest of the tree by removing a single edge $e$

nodes.name: Root $h_C$ of a clan
nodes.statement: The node $h_C \in C$ that is at one end of the edge $e$ is defined as the root of the smallest subtree that includes $C$.

nodes.name: Clans (E,F) and (E,F,G) of the Figure 1 tree
nodes.statement: For example, for the species tree in Figure \ref{fig:ils_hgt}, the sets of nodes $(E, F)$ and $(E, F, G)$ form clans in $\mathcal T$.

nodes.name: SDSR (Spectral Divide-and-conquer Species tree Reconstruction)
nodes.statement: \caption{\texttt{SDSR}} \begin{algorithmic} \Require Gene alignments $\{X^{g}\}_{g=1}^K$ for a set of species $C$, threshold $\tau$, tree reconstruction subroutine, minimum partition ratio $\beta$. \Ensure Reconstructed species tree. \State For every gene, compute an estimated distance matrix $\hat D^{g}$, its similarity matrix $S^g$ via Eq. \eqref{eq:similarity}, and the Laplacian $L^{g}$ by Eq. \eqref{eq:laplacians}. Then, compute the average Laplacian $\bar L$ via Eq. \eqref{eq:average_laplacian}. \State Compute a partition $C_1,C_2$ of the set of species $C$ by constrained $k$-means with minimum size $\beta |C|$ on the Fiedler vector of $\bar L$. \State Select outgroups $O_1 \in C_1$ and $O_2 \in C_2$ and set $\tilde C_1 = C_1 \cup \{O_2\}$ and $\tilde C_2 = C_2 \cup \{O_1\}$. \For{i = 1,2} \If{$|\tilde C_i|>\tau$} \State Apply \texttt{SDSR} to the subset of species $\tilde C_i$. \Else \State Recover subtree $\tilde {\mathcal T}_i$ by applying the tree reconstruction subroutine to species $\tilde C_i$. \EndIf \EndFor \State Let $h_1$ and $h_2$ be nodes in $\tilde {\mathcal T}_1$ and $\tilde T_2$ connected to $O_2$ and to $O_1$, respectively. \State Remove the outgroups $O_2,O_1$ from $\tilde {\mathcal T}_1$, $\tilde T_2$. \State Compute a merged tree $\hat{\mathcal T}$ by adding an edge between $h_1,h_2$ in the two subtrees $\tilde {\mathcal T}_1,\tilde {\mathcal T}_2$. \State \Return merged tree $\hat{\mathcal T}$. \end{algorithmic}
input: Gene alignments $\{X^{g}\}_{g=1}^K$ for a set of species $C$
nodes.statement_short: Recursively split species by constrained k-means on the Fiedler vector of the averaged gene Laplacian, rebuild small subsets with a base method, and merge the subtrees via outgroups.
also_stated_at: The input to \texttt{SDSR} consists of a set of $K$ gene alignments $\{X^{g}\}_{g=1}^K$, a threshold $\tau$, and a user-chosen species tree reconstruction method to recover the subtrees, which we refer to as a subroutine. The algorithm is recursive, and consists of four basic steps: (i) Partition the terminal nodes into two disjoint subsets $C_1,C_2$. (ii) Add to $C_2$ an outgroup node $O_1\in C_1$ and vice versa. Let $\tilde C_1 = C_1 \cup \{O_2\}$ and $\tilde C_2 = C_2 \cup \{O_1\}$. (iii) For each $i=1,2$, reconstruct the tree of $\tilde C_i$ as follows: if $|\tilde C_i|>\tau$, recursively apply \texttt{SDSR}. Otherwise, recover its species tree by the subroutine. (iv) Merge the two subtrees computed in (iii).
nodes.label: alg:cap

nodes.name: Averaged Laplacian
nodes.statement: For every gene, compute an estimated distance matrix $\hat D^{g}$, its similarity matrix $S^g$ via Eq. \eqref{eq:similarity}, and the Laplacian $L^{g}$ by Eq. \eqref{eq:laplacians}. Then, compute the average Laplacian $\bar L$ via Eq. \eqref{eq:average_laplacian}.
nodes.statement_short: Compute per-gene distances, similarities and Laplacians, and their average $\bar L$.

nodes.name: Spectral partition
nodes.statement: Compute a partition $C_1,C_2$ of the set of species $C$ by constrained $k$-means with minimum size $\beta |C|$ on the Fiedler vector of $\bar L$.
nodes.statement_short: Split species by size-constrained k-means on the Fiedler vector of $\bar L$.

nodes.name: Outgroups
nodes.statement: Select outgroups $O_1 \in C_1$ and $O_2 \in C_2$ and set $\tilde C_1 = C_1 \cup \{O_2\}$ and $\tilde C_2 = C_2 \cup \{O_1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick one outgroup from each side and add it to the other side.

nodes.name: Loop over subsets
nodes.statement: \For{i = 1,2} \If{$|\tilde C_i|>\tau$} \State Apply \texttt{SDSR} to the subset of species $\tilde C_i$. \Else \State Recover subtree $\tilde {\mathcal T}_i$ by applying the tree reconstruction subroutine to species $\tilde C_i$. \EndIf

nodes.name: Size test
nodes.statement: \If{$|\tilde C_i|>\tau$} \State Apply \texttt{SDSR} to the subset of species $\tilde C_i$.

nodes.name: Recursive call
nodes.statement: Apply \texttt{SDSR} to the subset of species $\tilde C_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Recurse on the subset.

nodes.name: Else
nodes.statement: \Else \State Recover subtree $\tilde {\mathcal T}_i$ by applying the tree reconstruction subroutine to species $\tilde C_i$.

nodes.name: Base reconstruction
nodes.statement: Recover subtree $\tilde {\mathcal T}_i$ by applying the tree reconstruction subroutine to species $\tilde C_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct the small subtree with the base method.

nodes.name: Subtree roots
nodes.statement: Let $h_1$ and $h_2$ be nodes in $\tilde {\mathcal T}_1$ and $\tilde T_2$ connected to $O_2$ and to $O_1$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Find the nodes adjacent to the outgroups (subtree roots).

nodes.name: Remove outgroups
nodes.statement: Remove the outgroups $O_2,O_1$ from $\tilde {\mathcal T}_1$, $\tilde T_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Delete the outgroups.

nodes.name: Merge
nodes.statement: Compute a merged tree $\hat{\mathcal T}$ by adding an edge between $h_1,h_2$ in the two subtrees $\tilde {\mathcal T}_1,\tilde {\mathcal T}_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Join the two subtrees by an edge between $h_1$ and $h_2$.

nodes.name: Return
nodes.statement: \Return merged tree $\hat{\mathcal T}$.

nodes.name: Averaged Laplacian $\bar L$
nodes.statement: We compute a gene-Laplacian matrix $L^{g}$ via Eq. \eqref{eq:laplacians}, and the averaged Laplacian, denoted $\bar L$, by \begin{equation} \bar L = \frac1K \sum_{g=1}^{K} L^{g}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Average of gene Laplacians
nodes.statement: \bar L = \frac1K \sum_{g=1}^{K} L^{g}.
nodes.label: eq:average_laplacian

nodes.name: Minimum partition ratio $\beta$
nodes.statement: Specifically, for an input set of species $C$ we add a constraint that the smaller subset is at least $\beta |C|$, for some value $0<\beta<0.5$.

nodes.name: Outgroup rooting
nodes.statement: As described below in step 4, the merging step relies on \textit{outgroup rooting} \cite{grant2019outgroup, boykin2010comparison}, a common approach to find the root of unrooted trees. The main idea is to reconstruct the tree with an additional species, related to but outside of the species group of interest. This added species serves as a reference point for the root's location.
nodes.statement_short: Root an unrooted tree by adding a related species outside the group; the root sits next to it.

nodes.name: SDSR outgroup selection
nodes.statement: Here, we select the outgroup according to the following simple procedure. Let $v\in \mathds R^m$ denote the Fiedler vector of $\bar L$ computed in Eq. \eqref{eq:average_laplacian}. We view distances in the Fiedler vector $|v_i-v_j|$ as indicative of distances between species $i$ and $j$. We choose $O_2 \in C_2$ by looking for the species whose average distance to the species in $C_1$ is closest to the average of all distances from $C_2$ to $C_1$. Namely, for each node $j \in C_2$ define $d_j = \frac{1}{|C_1|}\sum_{i \in C_1} |v_j - v_i|$ as the average distance from $j$ to the species in $C_1$ and by $D(C_1,C_2) = \frac{1}{|C_2|} \sum_{j \in C_2} d_j$. Let $\bar v^{(2)} = \frac{1}{|C_2|}\sum_{i \in C_2}^m v_i$ denote the average of the elements that correspond to $C_2$. By simple linear algebra \[ j = arg\,min_{j' \in C_2} |d_{j'} - D(C_1,C_2)| = arg\,min_{j' \in C_2} |v_{j'}-\bar v^{(2)}|. \] The outgroup $O_1 \in C_1$ is selected in a similar way.
nodes.statement_short: Choose as outgroup the species of the other side whose Fiedler entry is closest to that side's mean.

nodes.name: Fiedler distances
nodes.statement: Let $v\in \mathds R^m$ denote the Fiedler vector of $\bar L$ computed in Eq. \eqref{eq:average_laplacian}. We view distances in the Fiedler vector $|v_i-v_j|$ as indicative of distances between species $i$ and $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Use Fiedler-vector differences as species distances.

nodes.name: Selection criterion
nodes.statement: We choose $O_2 \in C_2$ by looking for the species whose average distance to the species in $C_1$ is closest to the average of all distances from $C_2$ to $C_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Criterion: average distance to $C_1$ closest to the mean cross distance.

nodes.name: Average distances
nodes.statement: Namely, for each node $j \in C_2$ define $d_j = \frac{1}{|C_1|}\sum_{i \in C_1} |v_j - v_i|$ as the average distance from $j$ to the species in $C_1$ and by $D(C_1,C_2) = \frac{1}{|C_2|} \sum_{j \in C_2} d_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $d_j$ and $D(C_1,C_2)$.

nodes.name: Closest to mean
nodes.statement: Let $\bar v^{(2)} = \frac{1}{|C_2|}\sum_{i \in C_2}^m v_i$ denote the average of the elements that correspond to $C_2$. By simple linear algebra \[ j = arg\,min_{j' \in C_2} |d_{j'} - D(C_1,C_2)| = arg\,min_{j' \in C_2} |v_{j'}-\bar v^{(2)}|. \]
nodes.statement_short: Equivalently pick $j$ minimizing $|v_j-\bar v^{(2)}|$.

nodes.name: Other outgroup
nodes.statement: The outgroup $O_1 \in C_1$ is selected in a similar way.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric choice of $O_1$.

nodes.name: Correctness of the outgroup merging step
nodes.statement: If the partitioning and recovery steps were accurate, then both subtrees, excluding their outgroups, form clans in the full tree $\mathcal T$. Thus, correct merging amounts to detecting for $\tilde {\mathcal T}_1$ and $\tilde {\mathcal T}_2$ the location of their respective root nodes.
assumptions: If the partitioning and recovery steps were accurate
conclusions: both subtrees, excluding their outgroups, form clans in the full tree $\mathcal T$

nodes.name: Differences between SDSR and STDR
nodes.statement: While the recursive structure of \texttt{SDSR} is similar to \texttt{STDR} \cite{aizenbud2021spectral}, we incorporate significant changes to all of the steps in the algorithm. (i) Unlike \texttt{STDR}, which reconstructs a tree from a single gene alignment, \texttt{SDSR} addresses the challenge of tree reconstruction by merging information from multiple genes. (ii) In \texttt{SDSR}, we partition the species by applying constrained $k$-means to the Fiedler vector. This procedure often yields more accurate partitions that those obtained with the sign pattern of the Fiedler vector. (iii) In \texttt{STDR}, the root was determined via a score function computed for all edges of the subtrees. The merging step in \texttt{SDSR} is based on an outgroup approach, which we found to be more accurate and requires fewer computations.
nodes.statement_short: SDSR differs from STDR by using many genes, constrained k-means partitions, and outgroup-based merging.

nodes.name: Cost of computing the similarity matrices
nodes.statement: Regarding the first part, computing $K$ similarity matrices from gene alignments of size $m \times n$ requires $\mathcal{O}(Km^2n)$ operations.

nodes.name: Argument for the per-iteration cost
nodes.statement: Partitioning the $m$ species requires computing the Fiedler vector of a positive semi-definite Laplacian matrix, which has a complexity of $\mathcal{O}(m^2)$ \cite[Chapter 2]{stewart2001}. Applying the outgroup approach in the merging step involves identifying the node adjacent to the outgroup in each subtree, removing the outgroup nodes, and adding a single connecting edge between the subtrees. The complexity of these operations is linear in the number of terminal nodes.
nodes.statement_short: Fiedler vector costs $O(m^2)$; outgroup merging is linear in $m$.

nodes.name: Fiedler cost
nodes.statement: Partitioning the $m$ species requires computing the Fiedler vector of a positive semi-definite Laplacian matrix, which has a complexity of $\mathcal{O}(m^2)$ \cite[Chapter 2]{stewart2001}.
nodes.statement_short: Fiedler vector computation is $O(m^2)$.

nodes.name: Merge cost
nodes.statement: Applying the outgroup approach in the merging step involves identifying the node adjacent to the outgroup in each subtree, removing the outgroup nodes, and adding a single connecting edge between the subtrees. The complexity of these operations is linear in the number of terminal nodes.
nodes.statement_short: Merging operations are linear in $m$.

nodes.name: Per-iteration partition and merge cost $O(m^2)$
nodes.statement: Thus, the complexity of the partition and merging step \textit{for a single iteration}, given the reconstructed subtrees, is $\mathcal{O}(m^2)$.

nodes.name: Partition-and-merge complexity $T(m)$
nodes.statement: Let $T(m)$ denote the complexity of all partitioning and merging operations.

nodes.name: Balanced-partition justification of the recurrence
nodes.statement: Given an input of $m$ species, the partition satisfies $\min(|C_1|,|C_2|) \geq \beta m$, for some constant $0<\beta \leq 0.5$.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides have at least $\beta m$ species by the k-means constraint.

nodes.name: Recurrence for $T(m)$
nodes.statement: Thus, the complexity of recursively reconstructing a tree from $m$ terminal nodes satisfies the following formula, \begin{equation} T(m) \leq \max_{\beta \leq \beta' \leq 0.5}T(\beta' m) + T( (1-\beta')m) + C m^2, \end{equation} for some constant $C$.
assumptions: Given an input of $m$ species, the partition satisfies $\min(|C_1|,|C_2|) \geq \beta m$, for some constant $0<\beta \leq 0.5$.
conclusions: T(m) \leq \max_{\beta \leq \beta' \leq 0.5}T(\beta' m) + T( (1-\beta')m) + C m^2,

nodes.name: Complexity recurrence
nodes.statement: T(m) \leq \max_{\beta \leq \beta' \leq 0.5}T(\beta' m) + T( (1-\beta')m) + C m^2,
nodes.label: eq:recurrence

nodes.name: Partition-and-merge complexity $T(m)=O(m^2)$
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:complexity_k2logk} in Appendix \ref{sec:complexity_appendix}, the complexity $T(m)$ may be bounded by \[ T(m) = \mathcal{O}\Big(m^2 \Big), \] where the multiplicative constant hidden in the $\mathcal{O}\bigl(\cdot\bigr)$ notation depends on $\beta$.
conclusions: the complexity $T(m)$ may be bounded by \[ T(m) = \mathcal{O}\Big(m^2 \Big), \]

nodes.name: Counting the small subtrees
nodes.statement: Given a threshold $\tau$ for the partitioning step, the smallest possible subset size is $\tau \beta$. Thus, the maximal number of subsets is bounded by $m/(\tau \beta)$. For each of these subsets we apply the user-defined tree reconstruction subroutine.
nodes.statement_short: Subsets have at least $\tau\beta$ species, so at most $m/(\tau\beta)$ subroutine calls.

nodes.name: Number of subsets
nodes.statement: Given a threshold $\tau$ for the partitioning step, the smallest possible subset size is $\tau \beta$. Thus, the maximal number of subsets is bounded by $m/(\tau \beta)$.
nodes.statement_short: Smallest subset $\tau\beta$, so at most $m/(\tau\beta)$ subsets.

nodes.name: One call per subset
nodes.statement: For each of these subsets we apply the user-defined tree reconstruction subroutine.
nodes.statement_short: One subroutine call per subset.

nodes.name: Subroutine complexity $f(\tau)$
nodes.statement: Let $f(\tau)$ denote the complexity of reconstructing a tree with $\tau$ terminal nodes via the user-chosen subroutine.

nodes.name: Cost of reconstructing all small trees
nodes.statement: The complexity of reconstructing all the small trees is thus $\mathcal{O}(m f(\tau)/\tau)$.

nodes.name: Overall complexity of SDSR
nodes.statement: Combining the complexity of all \texttt{SDSR} steps yields \begin{equation} \mathcal{O}\Big(Km^2n\Big) + \mathcal{O}\Big(m^2 \Big) + \mathcal{O}\Big (\frac{m}{\tau} f(\tau)\Big). \end{equation}

In this case, choosing $\tau=\sqrt{m}$ the complexity of the last term is $\mathcal{O}(m\sqrt{m})$, which represents a savings of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m})$ as compared to applying the algorithm to the full data.

nodes.name: Complexity of SDSR+CA-ML versus CA-ML
nodes.statement: We compare the complexity of \texttt{CA-ML} to the complexity of \texttt{SDSR} with \texttt{CA-ML} as subroutine. \texttt{CA-ML} methods compute a local maximum of the likelihood function of the concatenated matrix by \textit{hill climbing} iterations. The dominant factor in terms of complexity is the Subtree Pruning and Regrafting (SPR) moves, where a subtree is removed and re-attached at a different location. Testing all possible changes based on the concatenated dataset has a $\mathcal{O}(Km^2n)$ complexity for a single SPR move \cite{allman2005lecture, togkousidis2023adaptive}. This step is applied multiple times in many popular ML tools for tree reconstruction. In contrast, using \texttt{SDSR}, the cost of reconstructing the small subtrees via ML is only $\mathcal{O}(K\tau m n)$, a reduction by a factor of $m/\tau$. This reduction is achieved at the cost of computing the similarity, which is the dominating factor in \texttt{SDSR} with complexity of $\mathcal{O}(Km^2n)$. However, this operation is only done once, while SPR moves are performed multiple times in the hill-climbing process. Thus, the dominant term's complexity is reduced from $\mathcal{O}(Km^2n)$ to $\mathcal{O}(K\tau m n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Each SPR move costs $O(Km^2n)$ on the full data but $O(K\tau mn)$ in total over SDSR subsets, a factor $m/\tau$ saving.

nodes.name: Multispecies Coalescent (MSC) model
nodes.statement: Under the MSC, a gene tree $\mathcal T^g$ is randomly generated from the species tree according to the following bottom-up process. First, at time $\tau=0$ the gene tree starts with the same set of current species as in the species tree. Then, as time progresses, the species randomly coalesce to a common ancestor at a rate determined by the species tree topology and coalescence rates $\lambda (e)$ on its edges.

nodes.name: MSC coalescence conditions and excess time $\Delta^g_{ij}$
nodes.statement: The coalescence process satisfies the following two conditions: \begin{enumerate} \item $\tau^g_{ij}$ is larger than $\tau_{ij}$. \item Their difference, denoted $\Delta^g_{ij}= \tau^g_{ij}- \tau_{ij}$, has an exponential distribution with piecewise constant rates as follows. Let $h_{ij}$ be the MRCA of species $i,j$ in the species tree $\mathcal T$. Let $e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_\ell$ denote the path from $h_{ij}$ to the root of $\mathcal T$. Then, for each branch $e$ connecting a node $h$ to its parent $h'$, conditional on not having coalesced prior to time $\tau_h$, the coalescence rate is $\lambda(e)$. If no coalescence occurred before the root node, then beyond the root, there is a fixed rate $\lambda_0$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Substitution probability matrix $P_{h|h'}$
nodes.statement: The sequence generative process begins at the root, where its state is drawn according to some initial distribution over $\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d\}$. Then, for any parent node $h'$ connected by an edge to a child node $h$, the random variable $X_h$ is drawn conditionally on $X_{h'}$ via a substitution probability matrix $P_{h|h'}\in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$, \begin{equation} P_{h|h'}(l,l') = \Pr(X_{h} = \alpha_{l'} \mid X_{h'} = \alpha_{l}), \qquad \alpha_l, \alpha_{l'} \in \{\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_d\}. \end{equation} This process propagates from the root to the leaves. The observed sequences for each of the current species are generated by this process, independently for each location in the sequence.

nodes.name: General Time Reversal (GTR) model
nodes.statement: Under this model, the sequences mutate along the edges of the tree according to a continuous-time Markov process, with a rate matrix $Q\in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ that satisfies the following four properties: (i) $Q_{ij}\geq0$ for all $i\neq j$. (ii) each row of $Q$ sums to zero. (iii) there is a distribution vector $\pi\in\mathbb{R}^d$ with positive probabilities that satisfies $\pi Q=0$. (iv) $\text{diag}(\pi)Q$ is symmetric. Under the GTR model, the random variable $X_r$ at the root node $r$ of the tree is assumed to be distributed according to $\pi$.

nodes.name: Properties 1 and 2 hold under the MSC
nodes.statement: Note that under the MSC model, both properties 1 and 2 above indeed hold. Indeed, property 1 holds since the distribution of $\Delta^g_{i,j}$ and $\Delta^g_{i',j'}$ is determined by the edge parameters $\lambda(e)$ on the edges between the MRCA and the root, which are the same of both pairs. As for the second property, let $A$ be the event that the pair $i,j$ coalesce before $\tau_{i,l}$. In that case $\Delta_{i,j}^g< \tau_{i,l}-\tau_{i,j}$. Under the condition that $A$ did not occur, the MSC implies that the distribution of $\tau_{i,l}-\tau_{i,j} + \Delta_{i,l}^{g} $ is identical to that of $\Delta^g_{i,j}$. Since the probability of $A$ is positive, we conclude that the second property holds.

nodes.statement: The runtime results are consistent with the analysis in Section \ref{sec:complexity}. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: We prove the lemma by induction on the number of terminal nodes $m$. Our base case is a tree with two nodes $x_1,x_2$ where there is a single edge and a single non-diagonal element $W(1,2)$. Hence, one can simply assign the weight $W(1,2)$ to the edge $e(1,2)$ and thus satisfy the lemma. Next, we assume that the lemma holds for any tree with up to $m-1$ terminal nodes, and prove the claim for a tree $\mathcal T$ with $m$ nodes. We partition $\mathcal T$ into two rooted subtrees $\mathcal T_A$ and $\mathcal T_B$ by removing a single edge. Let $h_A$ and $h_B$ be the two root nodes of $\mathcal T_A$ and $\mathcal T_B$, respectively, and let $A$ and $B$ be their corresponding subsets of terminal nodes, see illustration in Figure \ref{fig:similarity_structure}. Accordingly, we partition the similarity matrix $W$ into four blocks: (i) The submatrix $W(A,A)$ which contains the pairwise similarity between nodes in $A$, (ii) The submatrix $W(B,B)$ which contains the pairwise similarity between nodes in $B$, and (iii) the matrices $W(A,B)$ and $W(B,A) = W(A,B)^T$ that contain similarities between nodes in $A$ and those in $B$. \begin{figure}[t] \centering \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{tree_rank_1_fig.png} \caption{A tree $\mathcal T$ and its corresponding similarity matrix $S$. On the right - the matrix block partitions used in the proof of lemma \ref{lem:weight_assignment}}. \end{figure} The four blocks of $S$ satisfy the following two properties with respect to the tree $\mathcal T$. \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item[\RNum{1}] The submatrix $W(A,B)$ is rank-1. \item[\RNum{2}] The submatrices $W(A,A),W(B,B)$ satisfy the rank-1 condition with respect to the trees $\mathcal T_A$ and $\mathcal T_B$ respectively. \end{itemize} Property I follows from the fact that $A$ and $B$ are clans of $\mathcal T$, and that by the assumption of the lemma $W$ satisfies the rank-1 condition with respect to $\mathcal T$. Hence there are vectors $v_A,v_B$ such that \begin{equation} W(A,B)= v_A v_B^T \end{equation} Property II follows from the above auxiliary Lemma \ref{lem:rank_1_submatrices}. By Property II and the induction hypothesis, we can set weights to the edges of $\mathcal T_A$ such that each element $W(i,j)$ where $(i,j) \in A$ equals the product of weights along the path between nodes $x_i$ and $x_j$. Similarly, we can set such weights to $T_B$. We denote by $w(A,h_A) \in \mathds R^{|A|}$ a vector whose entries are the product of weights along the paths between the subset of nodes $A$ and $h_A$. Similarly, let $w(B,h_B) \in \mathds R^{|B|}$ be denote the product of weights between the subset $B$ and $h_B$. Our proof is based on the following auxiliary lemma. \begin{lemma} The vectors $w(A,h_A)$ and $w(B,h_B)$ are proportional to $v_A$ and $v_B$ defined in Eq. \eqref{eq:v_AB}. Namely, \[ w(A,h_A) = c_A v_A, \qquad w(B,h_B) = c_B v_B , \] for some constants $c_A$ and $c_B$. \end{lemma} Lemma \ref{lem:rank_1_aux_lemma} relates properties \RNum{1} and \RNum{2}. For an arbitrary partition $A,B$, the singular vectors of the rank-1 submatrix $W(A,B)$ are proportional to the weights $w(A,h_A)$ and $w(A,h_B)$. We first complete the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:weight_assignment} assuming Lemma \ref{lem:rank_1_aux_lemma} is correct. We set the weight $w(h_A,h_B)=c_Ac_B$. Thus, \[ w(A,h_A)w(h_A,h_B)w(h_B,B) = w(A,h_A)c_Ac_Bw(h_B,B) = v_A v_B^T = W(A,B). \] Finally, we prove that the product $c_Ac_B$ is smaller than 1. Consider a quartet of nodes $(i,j) \in A$ and $(i',j') \in B$ and consider the determinant of the following submatrix \[ \bigg| \begin{pmatrix} W(i,j) & W(i,j') \\ W(i',j) & W(i',j') \end{pmatrix} \bigg| = \bigg| \begin{pmatrix} w(i,h_A)w(h_A,j) & w(i,h_A)c_Ac_Bw(h_B,j') \\ w(j,h_A)c_Ac_Bw(h_B,i') & w(i',h_B)w(h_B,j') \end{pmatrix} \bigg| = W(i,j)W(i',j')(1-(c_Ac_B)^2). \] By the definition of the rank-1 matrix, we have that the determinant is positive, which implies that $c_Ac_B<1$. Together with property \RNum{2}, we found a set of weights such that $W(i,j) = w(x_i,x_j)$ for all pairs $(i,j)$ which proves Lemma \ref{lem:weight_assignment}. Let us now prove auxiliary Lemma \ref{lem:rank_1_aux_lemma}. Let $h_{A1},h_{A2}$ and $h_{B1},h_{B2}$ be two pairs of nodes adjacent to $h_A$ and $h_B$, respectively. We denote by $A_1,A_2$ a partition of $A$ according to the nodes closer to $h_{A1}$ and $h_{A2}$, see illustration in Figure \ref{fig:similarity_structure}. Consider the submatrix $W(A_1,A_2)$. By property \RNum{2}, we can set weights to $\mathcal T_A$ such that, \begin{equation} W(A_1,A_2) = w(A_1,h_A)w(h_A,A_2) = w(A_1,h_{A1})w(h_{A1},h_A)w(h_{A},h_{A2})w(h_{A2},A_2). \end{equation} Note that we have a degree of freedom in the choice of $w(h_{A1},h_A)$ and $w(h_{A},h_{A2})$ since multiplying one and dividing the other by a constant does not change the product of weights between any pair of nodes in $A$. We will use this degree of freedom shortly. Next, consider three submatrices: $W(A_1,A_2),W(A_1,B)$ and their concatenation $W(A_1, A_2 \cup B)$. All three submatrices are rank-1, $W(A_1,A_2)$ by Eq. \eqref{eq:s_a_1_a_2}, and $W(A_1,B)$ and $W(A_1, A_2 \cup B)$ since the matrices $W(A,A)$ and $W$ satisfy the rank-1 condition with respect to $\mathcal T_A$ and $\mathcal T$, respectively. Since $W(A_1, A_2 \cup B)$ is a concatenation of $W(A_1,A_2)$ and $W(A_1,B)$, it implies that all three submatrices have the same left singular vector. By Eq. \eqref{eq:s_a_1_a_2} this singular vector is proportional to $w(A_1,h_{A1})$. We can apply a similar reasoning with the three matrices $W(A_2,A_1),W(A_2,B)$ and $W(A_2,A_1 \cup B)$ to conclude that the left singular vector of all three matrices is proportional to $w(A_2,h_{A2})$. We thus conclude that there are two constants $c_{A1}$ and $c_{A2}$ such that the left singular vector of $W(A_1,B)$ is equal to $c_{A1} w(A_1,h_{A1})$ and the left singular vector of $W(A_2,B)$ is equal to $c_{A2} w(A_2,h_{A2})$. The submatrix $W(A,B)$ is a concatenation of $W(A_1,B)$ and $W(A_2,B)$. Its left singular vector $v_A$ is thus a concatenation of $c_{A1} w(A_1,h_{A1})$ and $c_{A2} w(A_2,h_A)$. Recall that we have a degree of freedom for the choice of $w(h_{A1},h_A)$ and $w(h_{A2},h_A)$. We set the two weights such that \[ w(h_{A1},h_A) c_{A1} = w(h_{A2},h_{A2}) c_{A2} \equiv c_A. \] With these weights, $v_A$ is a concatenation of $c_A w(A_1,h_A)$ and $c_A w(A_2,h_B)$, which equals $c_A w(A,h_A)$. A similar reasoning yields that $v_B = c_B w(B,h_B)$ which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $m$: split at an edge, weight each side by induction, and set the cut-edge weight $c_Ac_B$ from the rank-1 cross block. Auxiliary Lemma 5 aligns the induced root weights with the singular vectors of $W(A,B)$.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: We prove the lemma by induction on the number of terminal nodes $m$. Our base case is a tree with two nodes $x_1,x_2$ where there is a single edge and a single non-diagonal element $W(1,2)$. Hence, one can simply assign the weight $W(1,2)$ to the edge $e(1,2)$ and thus satisfy the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Base case: two leaves, one edge of weight $W(1,2)$.

nodes.name: Split tree
nodes.statement: Next, we assume that the lemma holds for any tree with up to $m-1$ terminal nodes, and prove the claim for a tree $\mathcal T$ with $m$ nodes. We partition $\mathcal T$ into two rooted subtrees $\mathcal T_A$ and $\mathcal T_B$ by removing a single edge. Let $h_A$ and $h_B$ be the two root nodes of $\mathcal T_A$ and $\mathcal T_B$, respectively, and let $A$ and $B$ be their corresponding subsets of terminal nodes, see illustration in Figure \ref{fig:similarity_structure}. Accordingly, we partition the similarity matrix $W$ into four blocks: (i) The submatrix $W(A,A)$ which contains the pairwise similarity between nodes in $A$, (ii) The submatrix $W(B,B)$ which contains the pairwise similarity between nodes in $B$, and (iii) the matrices $W(A,B)$ and $W(B,A) = W(A,B)^T$ that contain similarities between nodes in $A$ and those in $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: split $\mathcal T$ at an edge into $\mathcal T_A,\mathcal T_B$ and block $W$.

nodes.name: Block properties
nodes.statement: The four blocks of $S$ satisfy the following two properties with respect to the tree $\mathcal T$.
nodes.statement_short: Two block properties follow.

nodes.name: Property I
nodes.statement: [\RNum{1}] The submatrix $W(A,B)$ is rank-1.
nodes.statement_short: Property I: cross block rank one.

nodes.name: Property II
nodes.statement: [\RNum{2}] The submatrices $W(A,A),W(B,B)$ satisfy the rank-1 condition with respect to the trees $\mathcal T_A$ and $\mathcal T_B$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Property II: diagonal blocks satisfy the rank-1 condition.

nodes.name: Justify properties
nodes.statement: Property I follows from the fact that $A$ and $B$ are clans of $\mathcal T$, and that by the assumption of the lemma $W$ satisfies the rank-1 condition with respect to $\mathcal T$. Hence there are vectors $v_A,v_B$ such that \begin{equation} W(A,B)= v_A v_B^T \end{equation} Property II follows from the above auxiliary Lemma \ref{lem:rank_1_submatrices}.
nodes.statement_short: Property I from the rank-1 condition ($W(A,B)=v_Av_B^T$); Property II from Lemma 4.

nodes.name: Apply hypothesis
nodes.statement: By Property II and the induction hypothesis, we can set weights to the edges of $\mathcal T_A$ such that each element $W(i,j)$ where $(i,j) \in A$ equals the product of weights along the path between nodes $x_i$ and $x_j$. Similarly, we can set such weights to $T_B$.
nodes.statement_short: Weight $\mathcal T_A$ and $\mathcal T_B$ by the induction hypothesis.

nodes.name: Root weight vectors
nodes.statement: We denote by $w(A,h_A) \in \mathds R^{|A|}$ a vector whose entries are the product of weights along the paths between the subset of nodes $A$ and $h_A$. Similarly, let $w(B,h_B) \in \mathds R^{|B|}$ be denote the product of weights between the subset $B$ and $h_B$.
nodes.statement_short: Root-to-leaf weight products $w(A,h_A)$, $w(B,h_B)$.

nodes.name: Auxiliary lemma
nodes.statement: Our proof is based on the following auxiliary lemma. \begin{lemma} The vectors $w(A,h_A)$ and $w(B,h_B)$ are proportional to $v_A$ and $v_B$ defined in Eq. \eqref{eq:v_AB}. Namely, \[ w(A,h_A) = c_A v_A, \qquad w(B,h_B) = c_B v_B , \] for some constants $c_A$ and $c_B$. \end{lemma} Lemma \ref{lem:rank_1_aux_lemma} relates properties \RNum{1} and \RNum{2}. For an arbitrary partition $A,B$, the singular vectors of the rank-1 submatrix $W(A,B)$ are proportional to the weights $w(A,h_A)$ and $w(A,h_B)$.
nodes.statement_short: State auxiliary Lemma 5.

nodes.name: Cut-edge weight
nodes.statement: We first complete the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:weight_assignment} assuming Lemma \ref{lem:rank_1_aux_lemma} is correct. We set the weight $w(h_A,h_B)=c_Ac_B$. Thus, \[ w(A,h_A)w(h_A,h_B)w(h_B,B) = w(A,h_A)c_Ac_Bw(h_B,B) = v_A v_B^T = W(A,B). \]
nodes.statement_short: Set the cut-edge weight $c_Ac_B$, reproducing $W(A,B)$.

nodes.name: Weight below one
nodes.statement: Finally, we prove that the product $c_Ac_B$ is smaller than 1. Consider a quartet of nodes $(i,j) \in A$ and $(i',j') \in B$ and consider the determinant of the following submatrix \[ \bigg| \begin{pmatrix} W(i,j) & W(i,j') \\ W(i',j) & W(i',j') \end{pmatrix} \bigg| = \bigg| \begin{pmatrix} w(i,h_A)w(h_A,j) & w(i,h_A)c_Ac_Bw(h_B,j') \\ w(j,h_A)c_Ac_Bw(h_B,i') & w(i',h_B)w(h_B,j') \end{pmatrix} \bigg| = W(i,j)W(i',j')(1-(c_Ac_B)^2). \] By the definition of the rank-1 matrix, we have that the determinant is positive, which implies that $c_Ac_B<1$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $c_Ac_B<1$.

nodes.name: Quartet determinant
nodes.statement: Consider a quartet of nodes $(i,j) \in A$ and $(i',j') \in B$ and consider the determinant of the following submatrix \[ \bigg| \begin{pmatrix} W(i,j) & W(i,j') \\ W(i',j) & W(i',j') \end{pmatrix} \bigg| = \bigg| \begin{pmatrix} w(i,h_A)w(h_A,j) & w(i,h_A)c_Ac_Bw(h_B,j') \\ w(j,h_A)c_Ac_Bw(h_B,i') & w(i',h_B)w(h_B,j') \end{pmatrix} \bigg| = W(i,j)W(i',j')(1-(c_Ac_B)^2). \]
nodes.statement_short: A quartet 2x2 determinant equals $W(i,j)W(i',j')(1-(c_Ac_B)^2)$.

nodes.name: Conclude bound
nodes.statement: By the definition of the rank-1 matrix, we have that the determinant is positive, which implies that $c_Ac_B<1$.
nodes.statement_short: Positivity of the determinant gives $c_Ac_B<1$.

nodes.name: Conclude Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Together with property \RNum{2}, we found a set of weights such that $W(i,j) = w(x_i,x_j)$ for all pairs $(i,j)$ which proves Lemma \ref{lem:weight_assignment}.
nodes.statement_short: All path products match $W$.

nodes.name: Root weight vectors are proportional to the singular vectors of $W(A,B)$
nodes.statement: The vectors $w(A,h_A)$ and $w(B,h_B)$ are proportional to $v_A$ and $v_B$ defined in Eq. \eqref{eq:v_AB}. Namely, \[ w(A,h_A) = c_A v_A, \qquad w(B,h_B) = c_B v_B , \] for some constants $c_A$ and $c_B$.
conclusions: The vectors $w(A,h_A)$ and $w(B,h_B)$ are proportional to $v_A$ and $v_B$ defined in Eq. \eqref{eq:v_AB}.
nodes.statement_short: $w(A,h_A)=c_Av_A$ and $w(B,h_B)=c_Bv_B$ for constants $c_A,c_B$.
nodes.label: lem:rank_1_aux_lemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: Let us now prove auxiliary Lemma \ref{lem:rank_1_aux_lemma}. Let $h_{A1},h_{A2}$ and $h_{B1},h_{B2}$ be two pairs of nodes adjacent to $h_A$ and $h_B$, respectively. We denote by $A_1,A_2$ a partition of $A$ according to the nodes closer to $h_{A1}$ and $h_{A2}$, see illustration in Figure \ref{fig:similarity_structure}. Consider the submatrix $W(A_1,A_2)$. By property \RNum{2}, we can set weights to $\mathcal T_A$ such that, \begin{equation} W(A_1,A_2) = w(A_1,h_A)w(h_A,A_2) = w(A_1,h_{A1})w(h_{A1},h_A)w(h_{A},h_{A2})w(h_{A2},A_2). \end{equation} Note that we have a degree of freedom in the choice of $w(h_{A1},h_A)$ and $w(h_{A},h_{A2})$ since multiplying one and dividing the other by a constant does not change the product of weights between any pair of nodes in $A$. We will use this degree of freedom shortly. Next, consider three submatrices: $W(A_1,A_2),W(A_1,B)$ and their concatenation $W(A_1, A_2 \cup B)$. All three submatrices are rank-1, $W(A_1,A_2)$ by Eq. \eqref{eq:s_a_1_a_2}, and $W(A_1,B)$ and $W(A_1, A_2 \cup B)$ since the matrices $W(A,A)$ and $W$ satisfy the rank-1 condition with respect to $\mathcal T_A$ and $\mathcal T$, respectively. Since $W(A_1, A_2 \cup B)$ is a concatenation of $W(A_1,A_2)$ and $W(A_1,B)$, it implies that all three submatrices have the same left singular vector. By Eq. \eqref{eq:s_a_1_a_2} this singular vector is proportional to $w(A_1,h_{A1})$. We can apply a similar reasoning with the three matrices $W(A_2,A_1),W(A_2,B)$ and $W(A_2,A_1 \cup B)$ to conclude that the left singular vector of all three matrices is proportional to $w(A_2,h_{A2})$. We thus conclude that there are two constants $c_{A1}$ and $c_{A2}$ such that the left singular vector of $W(A_1,B)$ is equal to $c_{A1} w(A_1,h_{A1})$ and the left singular vector of $W(A_2,B)$ is equal to $c_{A2} w(A_2,h_{A2})$. The submatrix $W(A,B)$ is a concatenation of $W(A_1,B)$ and $W(A_2,B)$. Its left singular vector $v_A$ is thus a concatenation of $c_{A1} w(A_1,h_{A1})$ and $c_{A2} w(A_2,h_A)$. Recall that we have a degree of freedom for the choice of $w(h_{A1},h_A)$ and $w(h_{A2},h_A)$. We set the two weights such that \[ w(h_{A1},h_A) c_{A1} = w(h_{A2},h_{A2}) c_{A2} \equiv c_A. \] With these weights, $v_A$ is a concatenation of $c_A w(A_1,h_A)$ and $c_A w(A_2,h_B)$, which equals $c_A w(A,h_A)$. A similar reasoning yields that $v_B = c_B w(B,h_B)$ which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Concatenated rank-1 blocks share left singular vectors; use the free scaling of the two child edges of $h_A$ to match constants.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let us now prove auxiliary Lemma \ref{lem:rank_1_aux_lemma}. Let $h_{A1},h_{A2}$ and $h_{B1},h_{B2}$ be two pairs of nodes adjacent to $h_A$ and $h_B$, respectively. We denote by $A_1,A_2$ a partition of $A$ according to the nodes closer to $h_{A1}$ and $h_{A2}$, see illustration in Figure \ref{fig:similarity_structure}.
nodes.statement_short: Children of $h_A,h_B$ and the split $A=A_1\cup A_2$.

nodes.name: Factor block
nodes.statement: Consider the submatrix $W(A_1,A_2)$. By property \RNum{2}, we can set weights to $\mathcal T_A$ such that, \begin{equation} W(A_1,A_2) = w(A_1,h_A)w(h_A,A_2) = w(A_1,h_{A1})w(h_{A1},h_A)w(h_{A},h_{A2})w(h_{A2},A_2). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Factor $W(A_1,A_2)$ through $h_{A1},h_A,h_{A2}$.

nodes.name: Scaling freedom
nodes.statement: Note that we have a degree of freedom in the choice of $w(h_{A1},h_A)$ and $w(h_{A},h_{A2})$ since multiplying one and dividing the other by a constant does not change the product of weights between any pair of nodes in $A$. We will use this degree of freedom shortly.
nodes.statement_short: Scaling freedom between the two child edges of $h_A$.

nodes.name: Shared singular vector
nodes.statement: Next, consider three submatrices: $W(A_1,A_2),W(A_1,B)$ and their concatenation $W(A_1, A_2 \cup B)$. All three submatrices are rank-1, $W(A_1,A_2)$ by Eq. \eqref{eq:s_a_1_a_2}, and $W(A_1,B)$ and $W(A_1, A_2 \cup B)$ since the matrices $W(A,A)$ and $W$ satisfy the rank-1 condition with respect to $\mathcal T_A$ and $\mathcal T$, respectively. Since $W(A_1, A_2 \cup B)$ is a concatenation of $W(A_1,A_2)$ and $W(A_1,B)$, it implies that all three submatrices have the same left singular vector. By Eq. \eqref{eq:s_a_1_a_2} this singular vector is proportional to $w(A_1,h_{A1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Concatenated rank-1 blocks share a left singular vector $\propto w(A_1,h_{A1})$.

nodes.name: Second side
nodes.statement: We can apply a similar reasoning with the three matrices $W(A_2,A_1),W(A_2,B)$ and $W(A_2,A_1 \cup B)$ to conclude that the left singular vector of all three matrices is proportional to $w(A_2,h_{A2})$. We thus conclude that there are two constants $c_{A1}$ and $c_{A2}$ such that the left singular vector of $W(A_1,B)$ is equal to $c_{A1} w(A_1,h_{A1})$ and the left singular vector of $W(A_2,B)$ is equal to $c_{A2} w(A_2,h_{A2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Same for $A_2$; constants $c_{A1},c_{A2}$.

nodes.name: Fix constants
nodes.statement: The submatrix $W(A,B)$ is a concatenation of $W(A_1,B)$ and $W(A_2,B)$. Its left singular vector $v_A$ is thus a concatenation of $c_{A1} w(A_1,h_{A1})$ and $c_{A2} w(A_2,h_A)$. Recall that we have a degree of freedom for the choice of $w(h_{A1},h_A)$ and $w(h_{A2},h_A)$. We set the two weights such that \[ w(h_{A1},h_A) c_{A1} = w(h_{A2},h_{A2}) c_{A2} \equiv c_A. \] With these weights, $v_A$ is a concatenation of $c_A w(A_1,h_A)$ and $c_A w(A_2,h_B)$, which equals $c_A w(A,h_A)$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose edge weights so both constants equal $c_A$; then $v_A=c_Aw(A,h_A)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: A similar reasoning yields that $v_B = c_B w(B,h_B)$ which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric argument for $v_B$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Let $S(A,B)$ and $S^{g}(A,B)$ denote two similarity matrices between nodes in a subset $A$ and nodes in the complementary subset $B$ in the species tree and gene tree, respectively. In the following proof we first assume that $A$ and $B$ are clans, and hence by Lemma 3.1 in \cite{snj} $S(A,B)$ is rank-1. We prove that in this case, $\mathbb E[S^{g}(A,B)]$ is also rank-1. Then, we show that if $A$ is not a clan, then $\mathbb E[S^{g}(A,B)]$ is not rank-1. Assume $A$ and $B$ are clans obtained by disconnecting the edge between $h_A$ and its parent node, and let $i \in A, k \in B$ be a pair of nodes with similarity $S^g(i,k)$ in the gene tree. By Eq. multiplicity of the similarity \begin{equation} S^g(i,k) = \exp\big(-D^g(i,k)\big) = \exp\big(-D(i,k) - 2\Delta_{ik}\big) = S(i,k)\exp(-2\Delta_{ik}). \end{equation} Since $k$ is external to the clan $A$, all pairs that include a node $i \in A$ and node $k$ share the same common ancestor, i.e. $h_{i,k} = h_{A \cup \{k\}}$ for any $i \in A$. Thus, by property \ref{prop_1}, the distributions of $\Delta_{i,k}$, and hence the expectation $\mathbb E[\exp(-2\Delta_{i,k})]$ are the same for any node $i\in A$. Let $S(A,k)$ be a single column in $S(A,B)$ that contains the similarity values between $k$ and the subset $A$ in the species tree, and let $\mathbb E[S^g(A,k)]$ denote the expectation of the corresponding column in the gene tree. Eq. \eqref{eq:gene_sim} implies that $\mathbb E[S^g(A,k)]$ is equal, up to a multiplicative factor, to $S(A,k)$. The same holds for any node $k' \in B$. Since $S(A,B)$ is rank 1, then $\mathbb E[S^g(A,B)]$ is also rank-1. \begin{figure}[t] \centering \includegraphics[width = 0.4\linewidth]{tree_quartet.png} \hspace{2em} \includegraphics[width = 0.4\linewidth]{inverse_cdf.png} \caption{ Left: Illustration of a quartet tree. For part (b) of our proof, we show that if $A$ and $B$ are not clans, $S(A,B)$ is not rank 1. Right: key property \RNum{2}: The random variable $\Delta_{i,k} + D(h_{i,j},r)$ stochastically dominates $\Delta_{i,j}$.} \end{figure} Next, consider the case where the subset $A$ is not a clan in the species tree. There are at least two pairs $(i,k) \in A$ and $(j,l) \in B$ where $(i,j)$ and $(k,l)$ are siblings in the inner structure of the quartet in the species tree, see illustration in Fig. \ref{fig:quartet}. We denote by $r$ the MRCA of the quartet. Consider the $2 \times 2$ submatrix $\mathbb E[S^g(A,B)]$, \begin{equation} \mathbb E\Big[S^g\big((i,k),(j,l)\big)\Big] = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbb E[S^g(i,j)] & \mathbb E[S^g(i,l)] \\ \mathbb E[S^g(k,j)] & \mathbb E[S^g(k,l)] \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} Similar to Eq. \eqref{eq:gene_sim}, each element of this matrix can be expressed in the following form: \[ \mathbb E[S^g(i,j)] = S(i,j)\mathbb E[\exp(-2\Delta_{ij})]. \] In addition, by the multiplicativity property of the similarity measure we have \[ S(i,l) = S(i,h_{i,j})\exp\big(-D(h_{i,j},r)\big)\exp\big(-D(r,h_{k,l})\big)S(h_{k,l},l), \] \[ S(k,j) = S(k,h_{k,l})\exp\big(-D(h_{k,l},r)\big)\exp\big(-D(r,h_{i,j})\big)S(h_{i,j},j). \] Thus, \[ S(i,l)S(k,j) = S(i,j)S(k,l)\exp(-2D(h_{i,j},r))\exp(-2D(h_{k,l}, r)) \] The determinant of the submatrix in Eq. \eqref{eq:gene_submatrix} equals, \begin{align} &\mathbb E[S^g(i,j)]\mathbb E[S^g(k,l)]-\mathbb E[S^g(i,l)]\mathbb E[S^g(k,j)] \notag \\ &= S(i,j)S(k,l) \Big( \mathbb E[\exp\big(-2\Delta_{i,j}\big)]\mathbb E[\exp\big(-2\Delta_{k,l}\big)] \notag \\ &- \mathbb E[\exp\big(-2(D(h_{i,j},r)+\Delta_{i,l})\big)]\mathbb E[\exp\big(-2(D(h_{k,l},r)+\Delta_{k,j})\big)] \Big) \end{align} Consider the triplet $(i,j,l)$. The root node $r$ is an ancestor of $h_{i,j}$ and hence by property \ref{prop_2} it holds that $D(h_{i,j},r)+\Delta_{i,l}$ stochastically dominates $\Delta_{i,j}$. Since $\exp(-2 d)$ is a monotonically decreasing function in $d$, then \[ \mathbb E[\exp(-2(D(h_{i,j},r)+\Delta_{i,l}))] < \mathbb E[\exp(-2\Delta_{ij})]. \] Similarly, \[ \mathbb E[\exp(-2(D(h_{k,l},r)+\Delta_{k,j}))] < \mathbb E[\exp(-2\Delta_{k,l})]. \] Hence, the determinant of the submatrix is positive, which implies it is rank-2. Thus, $\mathbb E[S^g(A,B)]$ cannot be rank-1. To prove that the quartet condition holds, it suffices to show that the this condition is satisfied in any similarity matrix of a tree, whose weights are between $0$ and $1$. Consider a quartet $Q = ((i,j),(k,l))$ such that $(i,k)$ and $(j,l)$ are siblings in $\mathcal T_Q$, see Fig. \ref{fig:quartet}. We denote by $S(h_{i,j},h_{k,l})$ the similarity between the ancestor $h_{i,j}$ of $(i,j)$ and the ancestor $h_{k,l}$ of $(k,l)$. The determinant $|S((i,j),(k,l)|$ is equal to, \[ |S((i,j),(k,l)| = S(i,k)S(j,l) - S(i,l)S(j,k) = S(i,k)S(j,l)(1-S(h_{i,j},h_{k,l})^2). \] Since $0<S(h_{i,j},h_{k,l})<1$, the quartet is positive.
nodes.section: C.1 Proof of Lemma 2: $\mathbb E[S^{g}]$ satisfies the rank-1 and quartet conditions.
nodes.statement_short: Clan splits: expected cross similarities are column-rescaled species similarities, so rank one. Non-clan splits: Property 2 makes a quartet determinant positive.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: Let $S(A,B)$ and $S^{g}(A,B)$ denote two similarity matrices between nodes in a subset $A$ and nodes in the complementary subset $B$ in the species tree and gene tree, respectively. In the following proof we first assume that $A$ and $B$ are clans, and hence by Lemma 3.1 in \cite{snj} $S(A,B)$ is rank-1. We prove that in this case, $\mathbb E[S^{g}(A,B)]$ is also rank-1. Then, we show that if $A$ is not a clan, then $\mathbb E[S^{g}(A,B)]$ is not rank-1.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: clan splits give rank one, non-clan splits do not.
nodes.section: C.1 Proof of Lemma 2: $\mathbb E[S^{g}]$ satisfies the rank-1 and quartet conditions.

nodes.name: Clan case
nodes.statement: Assume $A$ and $B$ are clans obtained by disconnecting the edge between $h_A$ and its parent node, and let $i \in A, k \in B$ be a pair of nodes with similarity $S^g(i,k)$ in the gene tree. By Eq. multiplicity of the similarity \begin{equation} S^g(i,k) = \exp\big(-D^g(i,k)\big) = \exp\big(-D(i,k) - 2\Delta_{ik}\big) = S(i,k)\exp(-2\Delta_{ik}). \end{equation} Since $k$ is external to the clan $A$, all pairs that include a node $i \in A$ and node $k$ share the same common ancestor, i.e. $h_{i,k} = h_{A \cup \{k\}}$ for any $i \in A$. Thus, by property \ref{prop_1}, the distributions of $\Delta_{i,k}$, and hence the expectation $\mathbb E[\exp(-2\Delta_{i,k})]$ are the same for any node $i\in A$. Let $S(A,k)$ be a single column in $S(A,B)$ that contains the similarity values between $k$ and the subset $A$ in the species tree, and let $\mathbb E[S^g(A,k)]$ denote the expectation of the corresponding column in the gene tree. Eq. \eqref{eq:gene_sim} implies that $\mathbb E[S^g(A,k)]$ is equal, up to a multiplicative factor, to $S(A,k)$. The same holds for any node $k' \in B$. Since $S(A,B)$ is rank 1, then $\mathbb E[S^g(A,B)]$ is also rank-1.
nodes.statement_short: Case: $A,B$ clans.
nodes.section: C.1 Proof of Lemma 2: $\mathbb E[S^{g}]$ satisfies the rank-1 and quartet conditions.

nodes.name: Non-clan case
nodes.statement: Next, consider the case where the subset $A$ is not a clan in the species tree. There are at least two pairs $(i,k) \in A$ and $(j,l) \in B$ where $(i,j)$ and $(k,l)$ are siblings in the inner structure of the quartet in the species tree, see illustration in Fig. \ref{fig:quartet}. We denote by $r$ the MRCA of the quartet. Consider the $2 \times 2$ submatrix $\mathbb E[S^g(A,B)]$, \begin{equation} \mathbb E\Big[S^g\big((i,k),(j,l)\big)\Big] = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbb E[S^g(i,j)] & \mathbb E[S^g(i,l)] \\ \mathbb E[S^g(k,j)] & \mathbb E[S^g(k,l)] \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} Similar to Eq. \eqref{eq:gene_sim}, each element of this matrix can be expressed in the following form: \[ \mathbb E[S^g(i,j)] = S(i,j)\mathbb E[\exp(-2\Delta_{ij})]. \] In addition, by the multiplicativity property of the similarity measure we have \[ S(i,l) = S(i,h_{i,j})\exp\big(-D(h_{i,j},r)\big)\exp\big(-D(r,h_{k,l})\big)S(h_{k,l},l), \] \[ S(k,j) = S(k,h_{k,l})\exp\big(-D(h_{k,l},r)\big)\exp\big(-D(r,h_{i,j})\big)S(h_{i,j},j). \] Thus, \[ S(i,l)S(k,j) = S(i,j)S(k,l)\exp(-2D(h_{i,j},r))\exp(-2D(h_{k,l}, r)) \] The determinant of the submatrix in Eq. \eqref{eq:gene_submatrix} equals, \begin{align} &\mathbb E[S^g(i,j)]\mathbb E[S^g(k,l)]-\mathbb E[S^g(i,l)]\mathbb E[S^g(k,j)] \notag \\ &= S(i,j)S(k,l) \Big( \mathbb E[\exp\big(-2\Delta_{i,j}\big)]\mathbb E[\exp\big(-2\Delta_{k,l}\big)] \notag \\ &- \mathbb E[\exp\big(-2(D(h_{i,j},r)+\Delta_{i,l})\big)]\mathbb E[\exp\big(-2(D(h_{k,l},r)+\Delta_{k,j})\big)] \Big) \end{align} Consider the triplet $(i,j,l)$. The root node $r$ is an ancestor of $h_{i,j}$ and hence by property \ref{prop_2} it holds that $D(h_{i,j},r)+\Delta_{i,l}$ stochastically dominates $\Delta_{i,j}$. Since $\exp(-2 d)$ is a monotonically decreasing function in $d$, then \[ \mathbb E[\exp(-2(D(h_{i,j},r)+\Delta_{i,l}))] < \mathbb E[\exp(-2\Delta_{ij})]. \] Similarly, \[ \mathbb E[\exp(-2(D(h_{k,l},r)+\Delta_{k,j}))] < \mathbb E[\exp(-2\Delta_{k,l})]. \] Hence, the determinant of the submatrix is positive, which implies it is rank-2. Thus, $\mathbb E[S^g(A,B)]$ cannot be rank-1.
nodes.statement_short: Case: $A$ not a clan.
nodes.section: C.1 Proof of Lemma 2: $\mathbb E[S^{g}]$ satisfies the rank-1 and quartet conditions.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:population_mean}, $\mathbb E[S^{g}]$ satisfies the rank-1 condition with respect to $\mathcal T$, namely $\mathbb E[S^{g}] \in \mathcal W_{\mathcal T}$. Let $v$ denote the Fiedler vector of a graph whose weight matrix is equal to $\mathbb E[S^{g}]$. Since $\mathbb E[S^{g}] \in \mathcal W_{\mathcal T}$, Theorem \ref{thm:snj_stdr} implies that partitioning the species according to $v$ yields two clans. Let $\bar L$ be the Laplacian of a graph whose weight matrix equals the sample mean $\bar S = \frac1K \sum_{g=1}^K S^{g}$. We denote by $\hat v$ the corresponding Fiedler vector, and by $0 = \gamma_1<\gamma_2<\gamma_3$ the smallest eigenvalues of $\bar L$. By the Davis-Kahan theorem \cite{yu2015useful}, \begin{equation} \|\hat v-v\| \leq 2^{3/2}\frac{\|\bar L- \mathbb E[\bar L]\|}{\min(\gamma_2,\gamma_3-\gamma_2)}. \end{equation} By the law of large numbers $\bar S$ converges to $\mathbb E[S^{g}]$, and hence $\bar L$ to $\mathbb E[\bar L]$. Thus, the Davis-Kahan bound (r.h.s of Eq. \eqref{eq:davis_kahan}) converges to zero for $K \to \infty$. Since by assumption $\min_j |v(j)| > 0$, the sign pattern of $\hat v$ is the same as $v$ once the Davis-Kahan bound falls below $\min_j |v(j)|$. Thus, partitioning the terminal nodes according to the sign pattern of $\hat v$ yields the same subsets as that of $v$, and is guaranteed to yield two clans in the species tree.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2 + Theorem 2 give clans for the population Fiedler vector; Davis-Kahan and the law of large numbers transfer the sign pattern to $\bar S$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Assume that the conditions of Theorem \ref{thm:finite_gene_guarantee_v2} hold, and in particular that the number of genes $K$ satisfies Eq. \eqref{eq:RHS_bound}. To prove the corollary, is suffices to show that the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:finite_gene} is smaller than that of \eqref{eq:RHS_bound}. Since the RHS of Eq. \eqref{eq:finite_gene} depends in $\|S\|/\Delta(\mathcal T_E)$, we separately upper bound $\|S\|$ and $\frac{1}{\Delta(T_E)}$. To bound $\frac{1}{\Delta(\mathcal{T}_E)}$, we take the reciprocal of Eq. \eqref{eq:allowed_error_quantity}, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{\Delta(\mathcal{T}_E)} = \frac{\sqrt{\eta}\cdot 2^{3/2}(\sqrt{m}+1)}{\sqrt{m}} \cdot (S_{\min})^{-1} \cdot \max\left\{1, (1+\eta)\cdot \frac{s_r^2}{1 - s_r^2} \right\}. \end{equation} Next, we bound the maximum term in \eqref{eq:delta_inv_expanded}. Since $\eta > 1$ and $s_r<1$, \begin{equation} \max\left\{1, (1+\eta)\cdot \frac{s_r^2}{1 - s_r^2} \right\} \leq \frac{1+\eta}{1 - s_r^2}. \end{equation} Now, notice that $\frac{\sqrt{\eta}\cdot 2^{3/2}(\sqrt{m}+1)}{\sqrt{m}} \leq c \sqrt{\eta}$ for some constant $c$. Inserting this inequality and Eq. \eqref{eq:max_term_bound} into Eq. \eqref{eq:delta_inv_expanded} gives \begin{equation} \frac{1}{\Delta(\mathcal{T}_E)} \leq c_1\frac{\eta^{3/2}}{(1 - s_r^2)S_{\min}}, \end{equation} where $c_1$ is some constant. We now proceed to bounding the spectral norm $\|S\|$. By Equation~\eqref{eq:S_norm_bound} of Lemma \ref{lem:spec_norm_similarity_bnd}, \begin{equation} \|S\| \leq \begin{cases} 3/2 & \text{if } \xi \leq \tfrac{1}{2}, \\ c_2 \cdot m^{1 + \log_2 \xi} & \text{if } \xi > \tfrac{1}{2}. \end{cases} \end{equation} where $c_2$ is a universal constant. Next, since both $\|S\|\geq 1$ and $\frac{1}{\Delta(\mathcal{T}_E)}\geq 1$, it follows that $\frac{\|S\|}{\Delta(\mathcal{T}_E)}\leq\frac{\|S\|^2}{\Delta^2(\mathcal{T}_E)}$. Thus, the term in Eq. \eqref{eq:finite_gene} may be bounded as follows, \begin{equation} \left(\frac{\|S\|^2}{2\Delta^2(\mathcal{T}_E)}+\frac{2\|S\|}{3\Delta(\mathcal{T}_E)} \right)\leq \frac{7}{6}\frac{\|S\|^2}{\Delta^2(\mathcal{T}_E)}. \end{equation} Finally, combining equations \eqref{eq:delta_inv_final}, \eqref{eq:S_norm_bound2} and \eqref{eq:dominant_term} yields \[ \left(\frac{\|S\|^2}{2\Delta^2(\mathcal{T}_E)}+\frac{2\|S\|}{3\Delta(\mathcal{T}_E)} \right)\cdot \log\left(\frac{2m}{\epsilon}\right) \leq \begin{cases} C_1 \cdot \frac{\eta^{3}}{(1 - s_r^2)^2S^2_{\min}} \cdot \log(\tfrac{m}{\epsilon}) & \text{if } \xi \leq \tfrac{1}{2}, \\ C_2 \cdot \frac{\eta^{3}}{(1 - s_r^2)^2S^2_{\min}} \cdot m^{2 + 2\log_2 \xi}\cdot\log(\tfrac{m}{\epsilon}) & \text{if } \xi > \tfrac{1}{2}. \end{cases} \] where $C_1, C_2$ are absolute constants. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 10
nodes.statement: Recall that an ultrametric tree is a tree where all the leaves are at the same log-det distance from the root. Equivalently, in an ultrametric tree, the similarity between every leaf and the root is equal. We start with a property of ultrametric trees. Let $\mathcal T$ be a rooted tree with similarity $S$, and $C_l,C_r$ be the two clans induced by the removal of the root. Then, easy to see that \begin{equation} \mathcal T \text{ is ultrametric} \iff \forall i\in C_l, j\in C_r: \quad S_{ij}=s_0 , \end{equation} where $s_0$ is some constant. Next, let $\mathcal T$ be a species tree, $S^g$ a gene similarity matrix generated according to the MSC+GTR model, and $\mathcal T_E$ the tree corresponding to the matrix $\mathbb E[S^g]$. Recall $\mathcal T_E$ and $\mathcal T$ share the same topology, therefore $C_l,C_r$ are clans in both trees. By Eq. \eqref{eq:ultrametric}, it suffices to show that $\mathbb E[S^g_{ij}]=s_0$ for all $i\in C_l, j\in C_r$. By Eq. \eqref{eq:ultrametric}, since $\mathcal T$ is ultrametric, $S_{ij}=s_1$ for all $i \in C_l$ and $j \in C_r$, for some constant $s_1$. By the gene similarity under the GTR, Eq. \eqref{eq:GTR_similarity}, for any $i\in C_l, j\in C_r$, \begin{equation*} \mathbb E[S^g_{ij}] = \mathbb E[e^{4\text{tr}(Q)\tau^g_{ij}}] \end{equation*} Inserting $\tau^g_{ij}=\tau_{ij}+\Delta^g_{ij}$, and using the definition of the species similarity, Eq. \eqref{eq:GTR_similarity_species}, \begin{equation*} \mathbb E[S^g_{ij}] = \mathbb E[e^{4\text{tr}(Q)(\tau_{ij}+\Delta^g_{ij})}] =S_{ij} \mathbb E[e^{4\text{tr}(Q)\Delta^g_{ij}}] =s_1 \mathbb E[e^{4\text{tr}(Q)\Delta^g_{ij}}]. \end{equation*} It remains to claim that $\mathbb E[e^{4\text{tr}(Q)\Delta^g_{ij}}]$ is constant. Indeed, by the MSC model, $\{\Delta^g_{ij}\}$ are identically distributed for all $i\in C_l, j\in C_r$.
nodes.section: H.3 On the proof of Lemma~8
nodes.statement_short: Ultrametric iff constant cross-root similarity; $\mathbb E[S^g_{ij}]=S_{ij}\mathbb E[e^{4\mathrm{tr}(Q)\Delta^g_{ij}}]$ with identically distributed $\Delta^g_{ij}$.
